soil-class-089.title: Twelve names ending in -sol: the USDA soil orders
soil-class-089.text: Twelve names, each ending in -sol, sort the world's soils at the top of {{ref:soil-class-006}}. These are the USDA soil orders, and their criteria reflect major differences in how soils formed. Each order reflects distinct soil-forming processes and traits, shaped by climate, vegetation and mineral makeup. Many hinge on a diagnostic horizon, such as an argillic horizon of washed-in clay or a mollic epipedon, a deep, dark topsoil. Ranked by increasing development, they run {{ref:soil-class-094}}, {{ref:soil-class-100}}, {{ref:soil-class-093}}, {{ref:soil-class-101}}, {{ref:soil-class-090}}, {{ref:soil-class-099}}, {{ref:soil-class-104}} and {{ref:soil-class-103}}. {{ref:soil-class-098}} and {{ref:soil-class-106}} can appear at any stage. {{ref:soil-class-092}} and {{ref:soil-class-096}} complete the twelve. The least-developed order also covers the most ground: 16.3% of the world's ice-free land. Next come the desert order at 12.7%, the young-soil order at 9.9% and the clay-subsoil order at 9.6%. The volcanic-ash order is smallest, at 0.7%. Mountain soils, a mixture of orders or soil-free 'Rugged Mountains', make up the remaining 11.6%. The United States looks different. The dark-topsoil order leads there with 22.4% of ice-free land, and the clay-subsoil order follows with 14.5%. The tropical oxide-rich order covers less than 0.01%. The list has grown over time. The 1975 taxonomy recognized 10 orders; the 1999 second edition recognized 12.

soil-class-101.title: Mollisols, the deep dark soils of the grasslands
soil-class-101.text: No soil order grows more food than this one. Mollisols are the world's most agriculturally productive order, and among the most economically important. Their mark is a deep, dark surface horizon rich in organic matter and nutrients, called the mollic epipedon. It is typically 60 to 80 cm deep and usually has a soft, granular structure. It builds up slowly, from long-term additions of organic matter by roots. Mollisols must also have base saturation above 50%. They are common in grasslands, and they form in savannas and mountain valleys, as in Central Asia and the North American Great Plains. Fire long shaped those landscapes, while ants and earthworms churned the soil. The order covers about 7% of the world's ice-free land but 22.4% of the United States, more than any other order there. Little of its native grassland survives: a 2003 estimate found only 14 to 26 percent still relatively natural. A dark topsoil alone does not settle the name. Where shrink–swell clays rule, the soil keys out as a {{ref:soil-class-106}}. Where volcanic-ash traits take precedence, it becomes an {{ref:soil-class-092}}. In the WRB, Mollisols split into three groups, among them {{ref:soil-class-123}}. Their rise is tied to the cooling and drying of global climate in the Oligocene, Miocene and Pliocene. Fossil Mollisols are confidently known from the Eocene.

soil-class-090.title: Alfisols, fertile soils with a clay-rich subsoil
soil-class-090.text: Calcium, magnesium and potassium: an Alfisol keeps enough of all three to feed crops well. An Alfisol is a moderately leached soil with a clay-enriched subsoil and relatively high native fertility. It forms in semi-arid to humid areas, typically under hardwood forest, and must have an argillic, natric or kandic horizon. The name comes from 'alf', for aluminum (Al) and iron (Fe), a root inherited from the old pedalfer group. By definition an Alfisol has at least 35% base saturation. That threshold is the line against {{ref:soil-class-104}}, which are more leached and fall below 35%. Productive and abundant, Alfisols are among the most important orders for food and fiber. Yet Australian and African Alfisols lack nitrogen and phosphorus, and monsoonal ones acidify under heavy cultivation. They cover about one-tenth of the ice-free land, 9.6% globally and 14.5% of the U.S. They dominate areas such as the Ohio River basin, the Baltic region and Sudan. In eastern North America, Alfisols occur in glaciated areas, while their more leached neighbors lie south of the limit of maximum glaciation. Suborders follow wetness and climate: oxygen-depleted Aqualfs, cold Cryalfs, humid Udalfs, semiarid Ustalfs and Mediterranean Xeralfs. In the WRB most Alfisols fall in the {{ref:soil-class-133}} or {{ref:soil-class-132}} groups.

soil-class-106.title: Vertisols, the clay soils that plow themselves
soil-class-106.text: Some soils turn themselves over without a plow. A Vertisol is rich in expansive clays that crack deeply when dry and swell when wet. It is both a USDA order and a Reference Soil Group of the {{ref:soil-class-016}}. It needs more than 30% clay to 50 cm and usually has a mollic epipedon, the dark topsoil of a Mollisol. Vertisols form in clay-rich material, often from basic rocks such as basalt, in seasonally humid or erratic climates. Alternate shrinking and swelling mixes the soil, a process called argillipedoturbation. Some end up with a very deep A horizon and no B horizon, and the subsoil heaves up as gilgai. Colors range from gray or red to deep black. Australians speak of 'black earths', East Texans of 'black gumbo' and East Africans of 'black cotton' soils. Found between 50°N and 45°S, Vertisols dominate eastern Australia, India's Deccan Plateau, parts of Sudan, Ethiopia and Kenya and the lower Paraná. They cover 2.4% of the world's ice-free land. The heavy, unstable soil makes it hard for trees to grow, so the natural cover is grassland, savanna or grassy woodland. Very hard when dry and sticky when wet, Vertisols are hard to farm without irrigation, and most are grazed by cattle or sheep. Their near-impermeability when saturated suits rice. Shrink–swell damages buildings and roads, but it lets the soil recover quickly from compaction. Australians, who call them Vertosols, prize them as among the few soils not acutely short of phosphorus.

soil-class-092.title: Andisols, the young, fertile soils of volcanic ash
soil-class-092.text: Wet rice on Java feeds some of the world's densest populations, and it grows on volcanic ash. An Andisol is a soil formed in such ash, rich in glass and in amorphous colloids such as allophane, imogolite and ferrihydrite. To qualify it must have andic properties: abundant poorly crystalline iron and aluminum minerals, high phosphorus, low bulk density and high organic matter. Being generally young, Andisols are usually very fertile. The exception comes where phosphorus is easily fixed, as sometimes happens in the tropics. That fertility supports intensive use. Besides Java's rice, Andisols grow fruit, maize, tea, coffee or tobacco, and those of the Pacific Northwest carry very productive forests. They cover about 1% of the world's ice-free land, mostly around the Pacific Ring of Fire. The belt runs from Chile and Mexico to Japan, Java and New Zealand's North Island. Suborders are wet Aquands, very cold Gelands, very dry Torrands, semiarid Ustands, dry-summer Xerands and young, glassy, coarse Vitrands. The WRB calls these soils {{ref:soil-class-119}}, though the two systems do not match exactly. Fossil Andisols occur far from present-day volcanoes. Some are dated to the Mesoproterozoic, 1.5 billion years ago.

soil-class-098.title: Histosols, soils built from organic matter
soil-class-098.text: Leave a waterlogged soil alone long enough and it can turn into coal. A Histosol is a soil made primarily of organic materials, recognized by both the WRB and USDA soil taxonomy. It has 40 cm or more of organic soil material starting within 40 cm of the surface. Organic material means at least 12% organic carbon in Soil Taxonomy, or 20% in the WRB. Histosols form wherever organic matter accumulates faster than it is destroyed. Usually poor drainage is the cause, because it prevents aerobic decay. Their materials grade from muck to {{ref:soil-class-070}}. Soil Taxonomy's suborders Saprists, Hemists and Fibrists follow those materials, alongside drier Folists and submerged Wassists. With {{ref:soil-class-096}}, Histosols store large quantities of organic carbon, which makes them ecologically very important. They have very low bulk density, and many are acidic and short of major nutrients. Rain-fed raised bogs, cut off from groundwater, are especially poor. Histosols are hard to cultivate. Drained ones on young glacial land can make good dairy or beef pasture. But dried organic matter can blow away as powder, and heavy structures subside. Most lie in Canada, Scandinavia, the West Siberian Plain, Sumatra, Borneo and New Guinea, and they cover 1.2% of the world's ice-free land. Australia calls them Organosols. As fossils they appear with the first extensive land vegetation, in the Devonian.

soil-class-093.title: Aridisols, the slow-forming soils of the deserts
soil-class-093.text: Deserts and dry shrublands make up about one-third of Earth's land surface, and Aridisols dominate them. Named from the Latin aridus, 'dry', they are the soils of arid and semi-arid climates, also called desert soils. Water shortage defines them. They have an aridic {{ref:soil-class-011}}, with fewer than 90 consecutive moist days in the growing season, and they are not leached. They also need enough age to show weathering in the subsoil, including some diagnostic subsurface horizon. An ochric epipedon is common. Sparse vegetation leaves them very low in organic matter, and soil formation is slow. Because little water passes through, the subsoil keeps what it gathers. Subsurface horizons collect deposited clay, sodium, calcium carbonate, gypsum or salts, sometimes cemented, as in caliche or duripans. Many have well-developed Bt horizons, built from clay moved down in past wetter periods. Salt building up at the surface can cause salinization. Aridisols cover 12.7% of the world's ice-free land. In the WRB most fall into four groups, including {{ref:soil-class-121}} and {{ref:soil-class-142}}.

soil-class-104.title: Ultisols, the red clay soils at the end of weathering
soil-class-104.text: The red clay of the Southern United States sits at the end of a very long road. Ultisols are strongly weathered, acid mineral soils, commonly known as red clay soils. The name comes from 'ultimate'. They were seen as the end product of continuous weathering in a humid climate, never renewed by glaciation. Taking hundreds of thousands of years to form, they stop sharply at the limit of maximum Pleistocene glaciation in North America. They hold no calcareous material, under 10% weatherable minerals in the top layer and under 35% base saturation throughout. They must also have an argillic or kandic horizon. Iron oxide colors them from purplish-red to pale yellowish-orange. They are typically quite acidic, often below pH 5, and kaolinite is often the main clay. Short of calcium and potassium, Ultisols need lime and fertilizer for settled farming. They are more easily exhausted than Alfisols or Mollisols, though organic-rich Humults are relatively fertile. Kaolinite has an upside: it gives good bearing capacity and no shrink–swell. Well-drained Ultisols such as the Cecil series therefore suit urban development. They dominate the Southern United States, southeastern China and Southeast Asia, and cover 8.5% of the world's ice-free land. In the WRB most are {{ref:soil-class-117}} or {{ref:soil-class-118}} soils.

soil-class-094.title: Entisols, soils that have barely begun
soil-class-094.text: The most common soil order on Earth is the one that has done the least. Entisols show no profile development beyond an A horizon and have no diagnostic horizons, so they are little changed from their parent material. They cover about 16% of the world's ice-free land, and 12.2% of the U.S. Many things can hold development back. The parent material may not weather, or erosion may strip the surface away. Floods, wind or slope processes may keep burying it under fresh deposits. Bedrock may lie shallow, or the material may be toxic, such as serpentine or mine spoil. So Entisols are common on river and beach sediments and on volcanic ash. Some are just an A horizon on bedrock. The suborders show the range. Aquents are saturated soils of riverbanks and mudflats, and Fluvents are alluvium renewed by floods. Shallow {{ref:soil-class-095}}, sandy {{ref:soil-class-108}} and Wassents, under water over 21 hours a day, complete the list. Entisols are so varied that their suborders match different WRB groups; Fluvents, for instance, correspond to {{ref:soil-class-126}}. In Australia most Entisols are called Rudosols or Tenosols. Most fossil soils from before land plants spread in the Silurian are Entisols. Unlike other orders, though, they reveal little about past climate.

soil-class-100.title: Inceptisols, young soils just starting a subsoil
soil-class-100.text: Between bare beginnings and maturity sits a large and varied order. Inceptisols are young soils with little to moderate development and weathering, more developed than Entisols. A B horizon has begun to form, but there is no diagnostic subsurface horizon of another order. Soils that fit no other order may default to Inceptisols. Profiles vary widely, but most have an ochric or umbric epipedon over a cambic horizon. Some have histic or plaggen epipedons, calcic horizons, duripans or fragipans. Inceptisols occur everywhere except extremes such as deserts and permafrost. They lie on mountains, sand dunes, fresh coastal and river deposits and late Pleistocene glacial drift. They also develop on eroded landscapes that, if stable, would have supported more developed Alfisols. Suborders follow temperature, moisture, saturation and epipedon: wet Aquepts, human-made {{ref:soil-found-110}}, cold Gelepts and Cryepts, humid Udepts, semiarid Ustepts and dry-summer Xerepts. Many crops grow on Inceptisols. Ustepts and Xerepts may need irrigation, and Aquepts need drainage. Aquepts with a sulfuric horizon are the exception, because draining them can produce sulfuric acid. Inceptisols cover 9.9% of global and 9.1% of U.S. ice-free land.

soil-class-103.title: Oxisols, the most weathered soils on Earth
soil-class-103.text: The oldest fossil Oxisols date from the first free oxygen in the atmosphere, about 2,200 million years ago. Oxisols are very highly weathered soils rich in iron and aluminum oxides, best known from tropical rainforest within 25 degrees of the Equator. They show the most profile development of any order. They must have an oxic horizon within 150 cm, and at all depths they hold no more than 10% weatherable minerals. Iron(III) and aluminum oxides and hydroxides make them always red or yellowish, alongside quartz and kaolin. The name comes from 'oxide'. Weathering, humification and mixing by animals form them. Rain, acidified by forest litter, leaches the minerals away, so plants depend on nutrients from decaying litter. Oxisols have a low cation exchange capacity, and their iron and aluminum oxides fix phosphorus strongly. Permanent cropping is therefore hard. Regions able to afford lime and fertilizer farm them intensively, as with Brazilian soybeans. Today Oxisols occur almost only in tropical South America and Africa, mostly on stable cratons. They cover 7.6% of global ice-free land but under 0.01% of the U.S. Suborders are wet Aquox, continuously humid Perox, humid Udox, semiarid Ustox and arid Torrox. Torrox are always paleosols from wetter times, mainly in Southern Africa. In the WRB Oxisols are mainly Ferralsols, and some were once classed as laterite soils. In warm periods such as the Mesozoic, they reached North America and Europe.

soil-class-096.title: Gelisols, soils over permanently frozen ground
soil-class-096.text: When frozen ground thaws, large structures subside. That makes permafrost a heavy limit on building, and it defines Gelisols, the soil order of very cold climates. Sources word the depth limit slightly differently. The order table requires permafrost within 100 cm, or cryoturbation within 100 cm plus permafrost within 200 cm. The name comes from the Latin gelare, 'to freeze', after the cryoturbation caused by alternate freezing and thawing. Organic matter builds up on top, so most Gelisols are black or dark brown over a shallow mineral layer. Calcium and potassium leach easily above the permafrost, which limits fertility. Slow decomposition makes these soils an important sink for carbon dioxide. Gelisols lie chiefly in Siberia, Alaska and Canada. Smaller areas lie in the Andes, Tibet, northern Scandinavia and ice-free Greenland and Antarctica. Together they cover 8.6% of the world's ice-free land. Gelisols key out before Histosols in soil taxonomy. Organic permafrost soils are therefore Histels there, but Cryic Histosols in the WRB, where most Gelisols are Cryosols. Fossil Gelisols are known from Precambrian ice ages 900 million years ago.

soil-class-108.title: Psamments, sandy soils that hold almost nothing
soil-class-108.text: The species-rich Fynbos of South Africa's Cape grows on sand that is extremely poor in nutrients. Such soils are Psamments, a suborder of Entisols made of unconsolidated sand. They occur in shifting dunes, or in very coarse parent material weathered for millions of years. A Psamment has no distinct horizons and must be loamy sand or coarser all the way through. The sand is poorly graded and constantly mixed, so it holds very little water. Being highly siliceous, it is extremely low in nutrients, especially phosphorus. It is also highly acidic, except in very arid climates. Young glacial Psamments of northern Europe are somewhat more fertile. Plants on them are often remarkably well adapted, as in the Fynbos and the Kwongan of Western Australia. Few Psamments are farmed. Fertilizing is costly, yields stay below other soils of the region, and the sand erodes very easily. Psamments cover 3.4% of the global land mass. They are abundant in the deserts of Africa and Australia, on old landforms of eastern South America and in Florida and Nebraska's Sand Hills. USDA soil taxonomy divides them by temperature and moisture regime into Cryopsamments, Torripsamments, Ustipsamments and Xeropsamments. Quartzipsamments, with over 90 percent resistant minerals, form a fifth group. In the WRB most are Arenosols, but those of river, lake or marine origin belong with {{ref:soil-class-126}}.

soil-class-111.title: Paleopedology, reading the soils of lost worlds
soil-class-111.text: Around 1795, observers in Scotland saw cliff soils that seemed to be remains of a former land surface. Paleopedology, the study of soils of past geological eras, began there. Its methods combine soil science and paleontology. Hilgard related soils to climate in the United States in 1892, and by the 1920s Glinka had found Russian soils that were relics of warmer climates. Fossil soils lie under sediment or volcanic ash, or where younger soil has eroded away, as in the Badlands of South Dakota. Buried soils lose their vegetation and organic matter. Yet the shape and size of root traces still reveal what grew on them. X-ray diffraction, developed since the 1960s, now lets paleosols be placed in the 12 soil orders. Many Precambrian soils fit no modern order. These 'green clays' are colored by unoxidized minerals that formed before free oxygen.

soil-class-095.title: Orthents, skeletal soils of steep slopes
soil-class-095.text: On very steep mountain slopes, erosion strips material too fast for deep soil to form. What remains is often an Orthent, a suborder of Entisols that lacks horizon development. Typically exceedingly shallow, Orthents are also called skeletal soils, or lithosols in the FAO classification. Any former soil has been removed or truncated. In Australia and parts of Africa they also occur on flat land whose rock has no weatherable minerals. They are unfit for arable farming and carry only low stocking rates, but they are important wildlife habitat. Many belong to the WRB's {{ref:soil-class-139}} or {{ref:soil-class-131}} groups.

soil-class-115.title: What fossil soils reveal about the history of land
soil-class-115.text: Very few fossil soils are of extinct types, unlike fossil plants and animals. That makes them useful for reading past ecosystems. The paleopedological record is chiefly paleosols buried by flood sediments or volcanic deposits, or preserved at geological unconformities. Burial changes them. Organic matter decays, iron oxidizes from Fe2+ to Fe3+ and hydrous ferric oxides dry out, so fossil soils grow harder to recognize. Telltale signs remain: downward-branching root traces, gradual alteration below a sharp former land surface, and crack patterns like peds and cutans. Most fit the twelve USDA orders, usually identified by X-ray diffraction. With little or no ozone layer, Precambrian soils eroded fast, and most are undeveloped Entisols or Inceptisols. Outside ice ages Oxisols have dominated the record, because new soil formation needs the glaciation and mountain building of cooler times. Land plants brought new orders: Histosols in the Devonian, then Alfisols and Ultisols. Mollisols spread only from the Miocene, as grasslands evolved.

soil-class-109.title: Sapric material, organic matter rotted past recognition
soil-class-109.text: In sapric material, decay has gone so far that plant parts and even fecal matter can no longer be identified. It is organic soil material of the kind found in a Histosol. The WRB defines it as having less than one-sixth of its volume as recognizable plant tissue within 100 cm. USDA soil taxonomy uses a fiber content below one-sixth. Muck is sapric soil that is naturally waterlogged or artificially drained. Canada places muck soils in its Organic order, with at least 30% organic matter and a depth of at least 40 cm. Sapric soils are deep, dark and friable, often underlain by {{ref:soil-fert-079}} or marly clay.

soil-class-102.title: Seven Mollisol suborders, sorted by water and warmth
soil-class-102.text: Water and warmth split Mollisols into seven suborders, set mainly by soil moisture and temperature regimes. Albolls and Aquolls are wet soils with an aquic moisture regime, and Albolls also have an eluvial horizon. Cryolls have a frigid or cryic temperature regime, and Gelolls a mean annual soil temperature below 0 °C. Udolls, Ustolls and Xerolls carry the udic, ustic and xeric moisture regimes of humid, subhumid and Mediterranean climates. Mollisol-like permafrost soils of Tibet and the Andean altiplano, called Molliturbels or Mollorthels, are not acidic. They make the best grazing land in those cold climates.

soil-class-091.title: Alfisols, the oldest forest soils
soil-class-091.text: The oldest forest soils on Earth are Alfisols, probably because of their fertility. Their fossil record reaches back to woodland and early forest soils of the Late Devonian. The oldest lie in the Aztec Siltstone of Victoria Land, Antarctica, with fossil wood and spores of Archaeopteris-Callixylon trees. Large woody roots pipe water and clay downward and leave material in the subsoil as they decay. That is the likely reason argillic horizons, Alfisols and forests go together. All tetrapod bones and tracks from Late Devonian and Mississippian paleosols of New York and Pennsylvania occur in Aridisols and Alfisols.

soil-class-107.title: Six Vertisol suborders, timed by their cracks
soil-class-107.text: Six USDA suborders sort Vertisols by wetness, temperature and how long their cracks stay open. Aquerts have aquic conditions and redoximorphic features. Slow permeability brings ponding. Cryerts, with a cryic regime, are most extensive in the Canadian Prairies. Xererts, with cracks open in summer and closed in winter, mark the eastern Mediterranean and California. Usterts, with cracks open at least 90 cumulative days a year, are the most extensive worldwide, though Torrerts lead in Australia. Uderts, with cracks open less than 90 days a year, are rare, mostly in Uruguay and eastern Argentina.

soil-class-105.title: Turning red clay Ultisols into garden soil
soil-class-105.text: A North Carolina Ultisol is roughly 82% mineral, 2% organic matter and 16% pore space. Gardeners aim for about 45% mineral, 5% organic matter and 50% pore space. Amendments are generally needed every year, guided by soil tests, and lime raises the pH. Mulch makes the soil more porous. Mixing 2 to 3 inches of compost and manure to a shovel's depth adds organic matter. Fall is best, so microbes release nutrients in time. Some gardeners skip amending with raised beds or {{ref:soil-fert-088}}, or grow native plants adapted to damp, poorly drained soils.

soil-class-116.title: More than 20,000 kinds of soil in one country
soil-class-116.text: The United States has identified over 20,000 soil series, each a unique kind of soil, classified in USDA soil taxonomy. Soil maps cover more than 95 percent of U.S. counties. Counting territories, Mollisols lead with an estimated 21.5% of the land. Alfisols follow at 14%, then Entisols at 12.3%, Inceptisols at 9.7% and Ultisols at 9.2%. Oxisols cover just 0.02%. Gelisols occur only in Alaska, and {{ref:soil-class-099}} lie under cool conifer forest and in Florida. Federal authority for mapping U.S. soils dates from the Agricultural Appropriations Act of 1896. Today the {{ref:soil-hist-051}}, led by the NRCS, carries it out.

soil-class-097.title: Histels, Turbels and Orthels: the three Gelisol suborders
soil-class-097.text: Gelisols split three ways, by how much frost has churned them. Histels resemble Histosols but have permafrost within two meters and 80% or more organic material in the top 50 cm. They dominate subarctic and low-arctic permafrost regions. Turbels show cryoturbation through more than a third of the {{ref:soil-env-146}}, with broken horizons, involutions, patterned ground and ice or sand wedges. They lie mainly in continuous permafrost. Orthels show little cryoturbation, affecting less than a third of that layer. They occur mainly in discontinuous permafrost and alpine areas. Churning is much stronger on exposed sites, where Turbels dominate, than in sheltered valleys.

soil-found-110.title: Anthrepts, Inceptisols marked by people
soil-found-110.text: Some soils carry the marks of long human use. Anthrepts are a suborder of Inceptisols in USDA soil taxonomy for soils showing evidence of human habitation and farming. They have a plaggen or anthropic epipedon, a surface horizon that signals intense and prolonged human activity.

soil-class-114.title: Finding the starting material of a fossil soil
soil-class-114.text: A soil starts out much like its parent material and loses its features over time. To judge how far formation went in a fossil soil, researchers need that starting point. They estimate the vanished parent material from nearby materials. Estimates rest on four assumptions. The proxy is fresh, it was uniform through the profile, at least one constituent survived weathering, and volume change tracks thickness and density. No constituent is fully immune to weathering. Quartz is fairly stable above pH 9, alumina between pH 4.5 and 8, and lead and zirconium over wider ranges.

soil-class-112.title: Soil climate, the weather inside the pores
soil-class-112.text: Every soil has a climate of its own, hidden in its pores. Soil climate is the moisture, temperature and other climatic conditions there, a special kind of microclimate. In well-drained soils it is a subdued version of the regional climate. In waterlogged soils it depends more on local groundwater than on the atmosphere. Classifying soils by climate data has been challenged by classifying them on observable features. The WRB counts soil climate only as a soil-forming factor. Climate-sensitive features let paleosols give a broad reading of past climate, though soils record it less precisely than instruments.

soil-class-113.title: Burrows, dung and roots: trace fossils in old soils
soil-class-113.text: A burrow, unlike a bone, usually stays where its maker lived. Trace fossils in paleosols are footprints, burrows, coprolites, or fossil dung, and root traces, all evidence of past organisms at work. They rarely identify a species, but their fixed position records behavior, as with the shallow burrows of solitary bees. Root-trace patterns and horizon sequences reveal the plant formation, such as forest, woodland or grassland, even when the species cannot be named. A paleosol can itself be seen as a trace fossil of a whole ancient ecosystem.

soil-class-110.title: Muck farming, vegetables from drained swamps
soil-class-110.text: Onions, carrots, celery and potatoes grow well on drained swamp. Muck farming works such soils of sapric organic matter, mostly for vegetables. It matters to farming in New York, Ohio, Illinois, Indiana, Michigan, Wisconsin and Florida. Torrey Farms' muckland at Elba, New York, is thought to be the world's largest continuous section. The 26,000 acres (10,400 ha) of the {{ref:soil-class-150}} are the largest U.S. concentration outside the Everglades. The light soil needs windbreaks and can burn underground for months. It also oxidizes away each year, growing shallower and releasing carbon dioxide. Because draining wetlands destroys habitat, muck farming is controversial. U.S. environmental regulations make new muckland unlikely.

soil-class-099.title: Spodosols, acid soils of the cool conifer forests
soil-class-099.text: Florida's most prominent soil order also lines the cool forests of southeastern Alaska. Spodosols are acid soils with a spodic horizon, where organic matter complexed with iron and aluminum has accumulated after leaching from the layer above. That horizon must lie within 2 m of the surface, and the soil must lack andic properties. Most Spodosols also have a bleached albic horizon. Their B horizon holds illuviated aluminum with organic matter, and often iron. They are typical of coniferous and boreal forests in cool, moist climates, such as southeastern Alaska and the Great Lakes. They cover 2.6% of global and 3.3% of U.S. ice-free land. They correspond to the {{ref:soil-class-138}} soils of Russia and northern and central Europe, and to Canada's Podzolic soils. Australia calls them Podosols. Spodosols are known only from the Carboniferous onward. Less acidic look-alikes from the Mesozoic and Tertiary may be an extinct suborder.

openers.usda-soil-orders: Twelve orders sort soils at the top level of USDA soil taxonomy, and this chapter meets them one by one. Their criteria reflect major differences in how soils formed. Some are young, with no development beyond an A horizon and little change from their parent material. Others are strongly weathered, from acid red clays to oxide-rich soils of the tropical rainforest. Between them lie deep, dark grassland soils, clays that crack when dry and swell when wet, soils of volcanic ash, soils made of organic materials, desert soils and soils over permafrost.

reviews.usda-soil-orders: The twelve orders run from barely changed Entisols to deeply weathered Oxisols, and diagnostic horizons do much of the sorting. A mollic epipedon marks Mollisols, a spodic horizon Spodosols, and 35% base saturation divides fertile Alfisols from more leached Ultisols. Climate and parent material shape the rest: Aridisols where water is short, Gelisols over permafrost, Andisols on volcanic ash, Histosols wherever organic matter outpaces decay. Suborders refine each order by moisture, temperature and, in Vertisols, how long the cracks stay open. Most fossil soils fit the same orders, so the record traces land plants from early forest Alfisols to Mollisols that spread with Miocene grasslands.
